passages.happening:
“Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy” (verse 1).

“For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God. Indeed, no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit” (verse 2). “But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort” (verse 3).

“The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church” (verse 4).

“I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy” (verse 5). The one who prophesies is greater, unless the one who speaks in a tongue interprets, so that the church may be built up.
passages.hearers:
Chapter 13 sits between chapters 12 and 14 for a reason. ‘Pursue love’ comes first. Then Paul turns love into a test for worship: what builds up the other person?

‘Edification’ is oikodomē, building up, literally building a house. It is the key word of this chapter. The Corinthians valued gifts that showed how spiritual they were. Paul values gifts that build others up.

Prophecy in the New Testament is speaking a message the Spirit gives, for others to hear in a language they understand. It is mostly not about foretelling the future. Paul says it brings ‘edification, encouragement, and comfort’ (verse 3). Later he says it can also bring hidden things to light (verse 25).

A tongue, as Paul describes it here, is speech addressed to God that others cannot understand unless it is interpreted. It is not worthless. The one who speaks is built up, and Paul wishes they all had the gift. But in the gathering it helps no one else unless it is put into words they know.

So Paul ranks the gifts by one test only: love for the rest of the church.
passages.ot:
Moses wished, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29), and Joel foresaw the day when God would pour out his Spirit and “Your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28). In the Old Testament a true prophet spoke God's word for God's people to hear: “let him who has My word speak it truthfully” (Jeremiah 23:28).

When Ezra read the Law to the people after the exile, the Levites helped them understand it: “explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8). Worship in Israel aimed at understanding, as Paul's does.
passages.asks: Paul measures every gift by whether it builds up others. Ask what you value most in worship: what moves you, or what helps the person beside you. And ask what it would look like to come to church next time asking how you can build someone up.

passages.happening:
If Paul came speaking in tongues, how would it help them, unless he brought revelation, knowledge, prophecy or teaching (verse 6)? A flute or harp must play distinct notes, and a trumpet must sound clearly, or no one will prepare for battle (verses 7-8). “Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air” (verse 9).

Every language has meaning, but if I do not know it, the speaker and I are foreigners to each other (verses 10-11). “Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church” (verse 12).

The one who speaks in a tongue should pray to interpret (verse 13). “For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful” (verse 14). So Paul will pray and sing with his spirit and with his mind (verse 15). Otherwise, how can an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving (verse 16)?

“I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue” (verses 18-19).
passages.hearers:
Corinth was a port city full of travellers. People heard languages they did not know every day. Paul uses that ordinary experience. Without understanding, a speaker and a hearer are ‘foreigners’, Greek barbaros, the word Greeks used for anyone whose speech sounded like nonsense to them.

‘Amen’ is a Hebrew word meaning ‘it is true’ or ‘so be it’. The early churches, Greek-speaking as they were, kept it. The whole gathering said it to agree with a prayer. Paul's point is simple: you cannot agree with a prayer you cannot understand.

Verse 18 is striking. Paul does not speak against tongues as someone who lacks the gift. He thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than any of them. He is not despising the gift. He is putting it in its place. In private, he prays in tongues. In the gathering, he chooses words others understand.

‘My spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful’ shows what Paul thinks happens when he prays in a tongue. His spirit truly prays to God. But his own understanding does not grasp the words, and no one else gains from them. So he wants both: prayer with the spirit and with the mind.
passages.ot:
Paul's pictures come from Israel's life. Trumpets called Israel to battle: “sound short blasts on the trumpets, and you will be remembered before the LORD your God” (Numbers 10:9). Joel says, “Blow the ram’s horn in Zion; sound the alarm on My holy mountain” (Joel 2:1). A muffled call was useless.

The psalms join heart and mind in praise. “Praise Him with the sound of the horn; praise Him with the harp and lyre” (Psalm 150:3). And the ‘Amen’ of the people runs through Israel's worship: at the end of the first book of Psalms, “Amen and Amen” (Psalm 41:13).
passages.hard:
What are the tongues Paul describes here?

Readers take them in two main ways. Some hold that they are real human languages that the speaker has never learned, as at Pentecost, where each hearer “heard them speaking his own language” (Acts 2:6). Paul's comparison with foreign languages in verses 10 and 11 fits that reading.

Others hold that they are a language of prayer given by the Spirit, not any human language, spoken to God (verse 2), and needing the gift of interpretation for anyone to understand. They point to ‘the tongues of men and of angels’ (13:1) and to ‘mysteries in the Spirit’ (verse 2). Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians speak of a ‘prayer language’ in this sense. Some readers think both kinds may be meant.

The site's notes on Acts 2 set out how Pentecostal, charismatic, continuationist and cessationist Christians read the gift and whether it continues today. These notes do not choose. All agree with Paul's rule for the gathering: what is said in public worship must build up the church.
passages.asks: Paul would rather speak five words that help others than ten thousand that impress them. Ask whether there is something in how you pray or speak about God that only you understand. And ask how you could put it into words that someone new could say ‘Amen’ to.

passages.happening:
“Brothers, stop thinking like children. In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature” (verse 20).

“It is written in the Law: ‘By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me, says the Lord’” (verse 21). So tongues are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers; prophecy is for believers (verse 22).

If the whole church speaks in tongues and outsiders or unbelievers come in, “will they not say that you are out of your minds?” (verse 23). But if everyone is prophesying and an unbeliever comes in, he will be convicted, the secrets of his heart laid bare, “So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, ‘God is truly among you!’” (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
Notice who is in the room. Paul expects that unbelievers and enquirers, the ‘uninstructed’, might walk into the church's gathering in a home. Worship was not hidden away. Outsiders could see and hear it.

Verse 22 can be confusing, since verses 23 to 25 seem to say the opposite: tongues drive unbelievers away, while prophecy wins them. Many readers explain it like this. In Isaiah, foreign speech was a sign of judgment on people who would not listen. Tongues without interpretation are the same kind of sign: they leave unbelievers outside, hearing only sounds, and they say ‘you are out of your minds’. Prophecy, in a language they understand, speaks to their hearts.

The scene in verse 25 is the goal of the chapter. A stranger hears God's word spoken plainly, sees his own heart, and falls down to worship. The church's worship should make an outsider say, ‘God is truly among you.’
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Isaiah, calling it ‘the Law’, a name for Scripture as a whole. In the BSB the verse reads, “Indeed, with mocking lips and foreign tongues, He will speak to this people” (Isaiah 28:11). Paul gives the words in his own form, close in sense but not word for word. In Isaiah, Israel would not listen to God's plain word through the prophets, so God would speak through the foreign tongue of Assyrian invaders: “But they would not listen” (Isaiah 28:12). Foreign speech was a sign of judgment on those who refused to hear.

The words of the converted outsider echo the prophets. Zechariah foresaw men of every nation saying to a Jew, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you” (Zechariah 8:23). Isaiah wrote that the nations will confess, “God is indeed with you, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:14).
passages.asks: Paul pictures a stranger walking into worship and meeting God. Ask what a newcomer would understand in your church's gathering. Would they hear only things they cannot follow, or plain words that reach their heart?

passages.t: ‘Not a God of disorder, but of peace’
passages.happening:
“What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church” (verse 26).

If anyone speaks in a tongue, only two or three, in turn, and someone must interpret (verse 27). If there is no interpreter, he should keep silent in the church and speak to himself and God (verse 28).

“Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said” (verse 29). If a revelation comes to someone seated, the first speaker should stop (verse 30). All can prophesy in turn, so that all learn and are encouraged (verse 31). “The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets” (verse 32).

“For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace” (verse 33), as in all the churches of the saints.
passages.hearers:
Verse 26 gives a picture of an early church meeting in a home. Many people took part: one with a psalm, one with a teaching, one with a revelation, one with a tongue, one with its interpretation. No single preacher is named. It was lively, and it could easily become chaotic.

Paul does not stop the gifts. He orders them. Speak in turn. Two or three at most. Let someone interpret. Let the others weigh what the prophets say.

‘Weigh carefully’ shows that prophecy in the church was not beyond question. Others tested what was said, to see whether it fit what God had already made known.

Verse 32 matters too. ‘The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.’ A Christian who speaks by the Spirit is not out of control. He can wait, stop or keep silent. The Spirit does not override a person.

Notice the word ‘silent’. Paul uses it here for the tongue-speaker with no interpreter (verse 28) and for the prophet who should stop for another (verse 30). He will use it again in verse 34. Each silence serves order and building up.
passages.ot:
The Law gave Israel a way to test a prophet: “When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken” (Deuteronomy 18:22). Paul's ‘weigh carefully’ continues that care.

God is a God of peace and order from the first page. In Genesis he brings order out of the deep, separating light from darkness and sea from land (Genesis 1). Israel's worship at the tabernacle was ordered with great care (Exodus 25 to 40). Paul's ‘not a God of disorder, but of peace’ draws on that whole picture.
passages.asks: In Corinth everyone brought something, and Paul asked only that it build others up and be done in order. Ask what you bring when your church gathers. And ask whether your freedom in worship ever crowds out someone else's.

passages.t: ‘Women are to be silent in the churches’
passages.happening:
“Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says” (verse 34).

“If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home; for it is dishonorable for a woman to speak in the church” (verse 35).

The book page lists these verses among the letter's hard passages. These notes say what Paul says, what makes the verses hard, and how Christians read them, without taking a side.
passages.hearers:
The puzzle is plain. In chapter 11 Paul expects women to pray and prophesy aloud in the gathering, and tells them how (11:5). So most readers agree that verse 34 cannot mean that women must make no sound at all in church. The question is what kind of speaking Paul means.

Notice the setting. These verses come straight after Paul's rules for weighing prophecies (verse 29), and they speak of women who ‘wish to inquire about something’ (verse 35). The silence is like the other silences in the chapter, which serve order.

Paul writes in a world of honour and shame. Philo, a Jewish writer of Paul's time, said that markets, council halls and law courts were for men, and the house for women. Many women had less schooling than men. Public speech by a wife in a mixed gathering could bring shame on her household. These customs are part of the background, though readers weigh them differently.

‘As the law says’ is not clear. No verse of the Old Testament tells women to be silent. Some readers think Paul has Genesis in mind, the order of creation or Genesis 3:16. Others think ‘the law’ here means a general principle of Scripture, or even Jewish or Roman custom.

There is also a question about the old copies. Every known Greek copy of the letter contains these verses. But in a few copies, of the group scholars call ‘Western’, they stand after verse 40 instead of here. Some scholars think the verses began as a note in the margin and were later copied into the text in two different places. Many others hold that they are Paul's own words, and that a copyist moved them.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament names women who spoke God's word. “Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time” (Judges 4:4). The king's officials went to Huldah the prophetess to ask what God said (2 Kings 22:14). Miriam is called “Miriam the prophetess” (Exodus 15:20). And Joel promised, “Your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28).

Some readers think Paul's ‘as the law says’ points to Genesis. After the fall, God said to the woman, “Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you” (Genesis 3:16). Others answer that this describes what sin brought, not God's command. Still others think Paul points to the order of creation in Genesis 2, as he does in 11:8-9.
passages.hard:
How do Christians read verses 34 and 35? These notes set out the main readings and do not choose.

Some read them as a limit on one kind of speech: women should not take part in the public weighing of prophecies in verse 29, which carried authority, while they still pray and prophesy. Others read them as dealing with disruptive questions in a gathering where many women had had less chance to learn; Paul's remedy is to ask at home. Others read them as a rule for that time and setting. Others read them as a general rule about authoritative teaching in the church, joined with “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet” (1 Timothy 2:12). A few read verses 34 and 35 as a Corinthian saying Paul quotes and then rejects with the sharp questions of verse 36. And some, as said above, think the verses were added by a later hand. For centuries many churches read them as forbidding women to speak, or at least to preach, in the gathering, and some still do.

From these readings Christians draw different conclusions.

Complementarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth before God, and that God has given them different roles in the church and the home, with the office of pastor or elder, and teaching the gathered church with that authority, given to qualified men. Many of them read these verses, with 1 Timothy 2, as limiting that kind of speech, and gladly see women praying, prophesying, teaching and serving in many other ways.

Egalitarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth and that every role in the church, including pastor and teacher, is open to both, as God gifts them. Many of them read these verses as dealing with a local problem of disorder, and point to 11:5, to Priscilla (Acts 18:26) and to Phoebe (Romans 16:1).

Both sides agree that women and men are equal in worth before God. Nothing in this passage permits anyone to demean women or to treat their voices as worth less.
passages.asks: Faithful churches read these verses differently. Ask how you hold your own view: with care for what Scripture says, and with respect for sisters and brothers who read it another way. And ask whether the women in your church are heard, honoured and given room to serve.

passages.happening:
“Did the word of God originate with you? Or are you the only ones it has reached?” (verse 36).

If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual, he should accept that what Paul writes “is the Lord’s command” (verse 37). “But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored” (verse 38).

“So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues” (verse 39). “But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Verse 36 is sharp. The Corinthians acted as if they could do as they liked, apart from the other churches. Paul reminds them that the gospel did not start with them, and they are not the only church. He has said again and again, ‘as in all the churches’.

Verse 38 is a warning. Some copies read ‘let him be ignorant’; most modern translations follow ‘he himself will be ignored’, meaning that God will not recognise one who will not recognise his word.

Verses 39 and 40 sum up the whole chapter in two lines. Be eager to prophesy. Do not forbid tongues. Do everything properly and in order. Paul wants the gifts, and he wants order. He does not choose one against the other.
passages.ot:
Paul's claim that his words are ‘the Lord's command’ stands in the line of the prophets, who spoke with the words “This is what the LORD says” (Isaiah 45:14). Moses gave God's commands to Israel at Sinai, and the prophets after him spoke God's word with his authority (Deuteronomy 18:18).

The Old Testament's worship joined joy and order. David brought the ark to Jerusalem dancing “with all his might before the LORD” (2 Samuel 6:14), yet he also set apart singers “to prophesy with the accompaniment of lyres, harps, and cymbals” (1 Chronicles 25:1), each in his place. Paul wants the same in Corinth: the Spirit's gifts, given freely, offered in good order.
passages.hard:
Does ‘do not forbid speaking in tongues’ (verse 39) settle the question of tongues today?

Christians read it in different ways. Pentecostal, charismatic and continuationist Christians read it as a standing command for the church in every age: tongues, with interpretation and in order, should not be forbidden. Cessationist Christians agree that it forbade the Corinthians to stop a gift God was then giving, but hold that tongues ceased with the age of the apostles, so the command does not apply to a gift no longer given. The site's notes on Acts 2 set out these views in their holders' own terms. These notes do not choose.

All agree with the last verse: whatever happens in worship ‘must be done in a proper and orderly manner’.
passages.asks: Paul ends with two commands held together: be eager for the gifts, and keep order. Ask which one you find easier, and which one your church leans toward. Then ask what it would look like to hold both, for the good of the whole body.
